unit.title: Verbs and Their Prepositions
unit.subtitle: Régimen preposicional: verbs that lock onto a fixed preposition

grammar.title: The preposition is part of the verb
grammar.intro: At C1, mastery is in the small words. Dozens of Spanish verbs govern a fixed preposition (régimen preposicional) that rarely maps onto the English one. You don't rely on someone, you cuentas con them; you don't dream about, you sueñas con. Worse, the same verb can change meaning with the preposition: pensar en (to think about) vs pensar de (to have an opinion of). Learn the verb and its preposition as a single unit.

sections.heading: Verbs governed by CON
sections.body: A cluster of very frequent verbs takes con where English uses on, about, or nothing at all. Notice how far the English preposition drifts:
conj: to put an end to / destroy

ex.es: Sé que puedo contar con vosotros pase lo que pase.
ex.en: I know I can rely on you come what may.
ex.note: contar con = rely on, not 'contar en'

ex.es: Tras horas de búsqueda, por fin di con la solución.
ex.en: After hours of searching, I finally hit upon the solution.
ex.note: dar con = to come across, stumble upon

sections.heading: EN and DE: where meaning shifts
sections.body: Several verbs demand en (insistir en, consistir en, fijarse en, tardar en, confiar en) or de (depender de, tratarse de, acordarse de). The trap is the pair pensar en (to have on your mind) vs pensar de (to hold an opinion), and acordarse de vs the transitive recordar (no preposition):

ex.es: No me acuerdo de su nombre, pero recuerdo su cara.
ex.en: I don't remember his name, but I remember his face.
ex.note: acordarse DE algo · recordar algo (no preposition)

ex.es: ¿Qué piensas de la propuesta? Yo llevo días pensando en ella.
ex.en: What do you think of the proposal? I've been thinking about it for days.
ex.note: pensar DE = opinion · pensar EN = have on your mind

sections.heading: Verbs governed by A
sections.body: Verbs of beginning, daring, giving up and refusal take a before an infinitive or noun. Atreverse a, renunciar a, negarse a and ponerse a are C1 staples:

ex.es: Se negó a firmar y renunció a su parte de la herencia.
ex.en: He refused to sign and gave up his share of the inheritance.
ex.note: negarse A + inf · renunciar A + noun

ex.es: Quedamos en vernos a las ocho, pero nadie se atrevió a llegar tarde.
ex.en: We agreed to meet at eight, but nobody dared to be late.
ex.note: quedar EN = to agree/arrange · atreverse A = to dare

takeaways: Learn verb + preposition as one chunk: contar con, soñar con, insistir en, depender de, atreverse a.
The Spanish preposition rarely mirrors English: rely ON = contar CON; dream ABOUT = soñar CON.
pensar EN = have on your mind; pensar DE = have an opinion of — different prepositions, different meanings.
acordarse DE algo = recordar algo (transitive, no preposition); quedar EN = to agree/arrange to.

mistakes.w: Cuento en ti para el proyecto.
mistakes.why: contar governs 'con', not 'en'; and con + ti fuses into 'contigo'.

mistakes.w: No me recuerdo de su nombre.
mistakes.r: No me acuerdo de su nombre.
mistakes.why: recordar is transitive (recordar algo); the pronominal verb that takes 'de' is acordarse de.

mistakes.w: Me negué de firmar el contrato.
mistakes.r: Me negué a firmar el contrato.
mistakes.why: negarse governs 'a' before the infinitive, not 'de'.

exercises.prompt: Puedes ___ nosotros para lo que necesites.
exercises.prompt_en: You can count on us for whatever you need.
exercises.no: ‘To rely on’ is contar CON, never contar en.

exercises.prompt: Todo ___ de que lleguemos a tiempo al aeropuerto.
exercises.prompt_en: Everything depends on our getting to the airport on time.
exercises.no: The verb that governs ‘de’ here is depender (depender de = to depend on).

exercises.prompt: Build: “We agreed to meet the following day.”
exercises.no: “Quedamos en vernos al día siguiente” — quedar governs EN, not de/con.

exercises.prompt: No me ___ dónde dejé las llaves.
exercises.prompt_en: I don't remember where I left the keys.
exercises.no: Use acordarse de: “No me acuerdo de dónde…”. (recordar would need no preposition.)

exercises.prompt: Match each verb to the preposition it governs.

exercises.tts: Insistió en pagar la cuenta él mismo.
accepted: insistio en pagar la cuenta el mismo
exercises.translation: He insisted on paying the bill himself.
exercises.ok: ¡Correcto! “Insistió en pagar la cuenta él mismo.”
exercises.no: It was: “Insistió en pagar la cuenta él mismo.” (insistir en = to insist on)

exercises.scenario: A colleague asks your view on a plan they can't stop mulling over 💭

lines.speaker: Elena
lines.es: Llevo toda la semana pensando en la reestructuración. ¿Tú qué piensas de ella?
lines.en: I've been thinking about the restructuring all week. What do you think of it?

options.text: Pienso que es arriesgada, pero puede salir bien.
Pienso en que es arriesgada, pero puede salir bien.
Pienso de que es arriesgada, pero puede salir bien.

exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! Para dar una opinión: pienso que… (o ¿qué piensas de…?).
exercises.no: To state an opinion you use ‘pienso que…’. ‘Pensar de’ appears in the question (¿qué piensas de…?), not before ‘que’.

exercises.en: I don't dare to contradict him.
exercises.no: Almost — tap “Hear it”, then match the sound of “No me atrevo a contradecirle.”
